clue.text: Gathering of women being quite upset about lecturer

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the next piece, as something put about it
upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of these two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A meeting of women gets agitated over the arrival of a lecturer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges BEING QUITE, and 'about' wraps those letters round L.
explanation.definitionFit: A quilting bee is an American social gathering, traditionally of women, who meet to sew quilts together.

clue.text: Question very overlooked by fair man

indicators.note: something overlooked is left out, so the letter for very is dropped from the next word

parts.note: fair means even, as in an even contest

explanation.surface: A question is ignored by a handsome man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair man' looks like one phrase, but 'fair' gives EVEN and 'man' alone is the definition, in its chess sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In chess every piece is called a man, and this is the most powerful one on the board.

clue.text: Drunk swilling a beer in it

indicators.note: swilling means sloshing liquid about, so these letters are swirled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tipsy is sloshing a beer around in a glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a person who is intoxicated by alcohol; the longer one is a formal synonym.

clue.text: Some acrobatic equipment split up with no difficulty, we hear

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: split means part, as in to split or part company

indicators.note: we hear signals that the letters built are spoken, and the answer sounds like them

parts.note: doing something with no difficulty is doing it with ease

explanation.surface: Circus gear divides up easily, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns PART into TRAP; 'we hear' turns EASE into its sound-alike ending, EZE.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging bar hung from ropes is a staple piece of kit for circus acrobats.

clue.text: Resurrection at hand? Not entirely, according to this prophet

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the words is used, so the answer sits inside them

explanation.surface: A religious remark: the resurrection is not quite at hand, says a prophet.
explanation.definitionFit: Nathan was an Old Testament prophet who rebuked King David over Bathsheba.

clue.text: Abandon something implied in 14?

definitions.meaning: to abandon a claim or position is to give it up, retreat from it
14 is a ballet named after swans, birds whose backs are covered in soft feathers

explanation.surface: Give up something hinted at by another entry.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it means retreat; read as two words it is the soft feathers on a swan's back, from the ballet at 14.
explanation.definitionFit: Retreating from a stance means giving it up; separately, swans have fluffy feathers on their backs.

clue.text: Dodging a positive answer to "Do you spend?" after reflection

indicators.note: reflection means mirroring, so the reply is read backwards

parts.words: a positive answer to "Do you spend?"
parts.note: a thrifty reply to that question is 'No, I save', positive in spirit though it starts with no

explanation.surface: Avoiding a straight reply to a question about spending, after some thought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after reflection' reverses NO I SAVE. 'positive' seems wrong for a reply starting 'No', but the reply is a virtuous one.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodging a question or duty is evasion, the act of slipping out of it.

clue.text: Police operation taking rear off vehicle

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter, which is removed

parts.note: a bust is a police raid

explanation.surface: A police raid strips the back off a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A public road vehicle carrying many passengers is the everyday sense here.

clue.text: Gets hot and stops, abandoning run

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so the letter for run goes

parts.note: a driver brakes to stop
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A runner overheats and halts, giving up the run.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, a person sweltering in heat is said to be baking, as if in an oven.

clue.text: Second attempt to secure patron, surprisingly

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the attempt holds the patron inside

parts.note: an attempt is a try
an angel is a financial backer, especially of a theatre production

explanation.surface: A second try at landing a sponsor goes, to everyone's surprise, well.
explanation.walkthrough: ANGEL as a theatre backer is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adverbs describe something happening in an odd or unexpected way.

clue.text: Intended to dismiss opener after cricket side put in? Neat

indicators.note: put in signals the cricket side going inside the shortened word
the opener is the first letter, dismissed as a cricket opening batsman would be

parts.note: intended means meant
the leg side is one half of a cricket field

explanation.surface: A cricketing scene: the plan to get rid of the opening batsman after the leg side was put in to bat looks tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface hides plain wordplay. The leg side is the half of a cricket field behind the batsman's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat can mean stylish and well turned out, which is a synonym for graceful, refined.

clue.text: Rather attractive individual you've pulled?

definitions.meaning: a knockout or stunner, British slang for a very good-looking person
a festive paper tube that two people tug apart with a bang at Christmas dinner

explanation.surface: Someone asks about the good-looking person you've picked up on a night out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulled' is British slang for attracting someone, but here it is a Christmas party novelty pulled in two.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls a gorgeous person this, and it is also a Christmas novelty that two people tug apart.

clue.text: Care attendant commented about me turning back after journey held over

indicators.note: after puts the commented piece behind the journey piece
held over means turned over, so the word for journey is read backwards

parts.note: a run is a short journey, as in a run to the shops

indicators.note: the word for commented goes around the turned word

parts.note: commented means said

indicators.note: turning back means the word me is read backwards

explanation.surface: A carer remarked on me heading home after a trip was postponed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held over' looks like postponement, but it turns the journey word round; 'after' fixes the order of the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman employed to look after young children is a carer or attendant for them.

clue.text: Cattle ailment covered by popular writer

indicators.note: covered by means wrapped inside, so the disease goes inside the word for popular

parts.note: popular things are in, in fashion
BSE is bovine spongiform encephalopathy, mad cow disease

explanation.surface: A cattle disease written up by a bestselling author.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright who wrote A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: They dig trenches over, covering both sides of dyke

indicators.note: covering means going around the next piece
over means turned over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a sap is a military trench dug towards an enemy position

indicators.note: both sides of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Diggers turn trenches over, covering both banks of a dyke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns SAPS into SPAS, which goes 'covering' DE, the outer letters of 'dyke'. SAP for trench is a military term.
explanation.definitionFit: These garden tools are what people use to dig soil, so they are the things that dig.

clue.text: Easy Phi worked out? Seen gutted about that, requiring unrelenting toil?

indicators.note: the two outer letters go about the rearranged letters
gutted means the inside is removed, leaving only the outer letters
worked out means solved or reshaped, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: Phi is the setter's pseudonym, used as written

explanation.surface: The setter boasts the puzzle is easily solved, yet it demanded endless toil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' leaves SN from 'Seen', set 'about' an arrangement of EASY PHI ('worked out').
explanation.definitionFit: Sisyphus was condemned to push a boulder uphill forever, so endless futile labour is named after him.

clue.text: Small late party when hosting a new line in ballet

indicators.note: hosting means having guests inside, so the wake contains the next letters

parts.note: a wake is a gathering held after a funeral, a party for the late person

explanation.surface: A small party late at night with a new line-up of guests during a ballet evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late party' is a funeral wake, not an all-nighter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's famous ballet tells of Odette, a princess turned into a swan.

clue.text: Scots own parks in a wholly historic part of France

indicators.note: parks in means settles inside, so the Scots word goes inside the next letters

parts.note: quite means wholly, as in quite right
ain is the Scots word for own, as in 'my ain folk'

explanation.surface: Scots have their own parks in a historic French region.
explanation.definitionFit: Aquitaine is a former duchy and province in south-west France, once ruled by English kings.

clue.text: Obsessive financial centre upset regarding diagnostics?

parts.note: anal is slang for obsessively fussy

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: An obsessive in the financial world gets upset about medical tests.
explanation.walkthrough: THE CITY is the City of London, Britain's banking district.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to analysis, and diagnostics is detailed analysis of a fault or illness.

clue.text: Carol, about to take off clothes, retiring — and doing this?

indicators.note: the singing word goes about the next piece

parts.note: to carol is to sing

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to peel is to strip off clothes

explanation.surface: Carol undresses before going to bed, and then what does she do?
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' reverses PEEL to LEEP, and SING goes 'about' it. 'Carol' looks like a name but is the verb. The definition leans on 'retiring' = going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who undresses and goes to bed is likely to be asleep soon after.

clue.text: Definite force seizing city

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold, so the force word holds the city

parts.note: to prise is to force open with a lever
EC is the postcode area for the City of London

explanation.surface: A sure force takes over a city.
explanation.walkthrough: EC is the City of London's postcode, so it stands for city.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something exact and clearly stated, with no vagueness.

clue.text: United in defeat — ultimate in generosity? That's a lovely thing to see

indicators.note: in means placed inside the next word

parts.note: to defeat is to beat
U is the abbreviation for United in team names

indicators.note: the ultimate letter of a word is its last

explanation.surface: A football fan's lament: United lose, but the gracious losers are a fine sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A beauty is something very pleasing to look at, an admirable example.

clue.text: Attention and skill capturing height for aviatrix

indicators.note: capturing means taking prisoner, so the letter for height goes inside

parts.note: to lend an ear is to pay attention
art means skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: Attention and skill help a pilot capture new heights.
explanation.definitionFit: Amelia Earhart was the American aviator who flew solo across the Atlantic and vanished in 1937.

clue.text: Start of month: picked up North American lizard

indicators.note: in a down clue picked up means lifted, so the letters are read upwards

parts.note: the first of August is written AUG I, using the roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: At the beginning of the month someone collected a lizard from America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' sounds like a homophone signal, but it reverses AUG I to IGUA.
explanation.definitionFit: The iguana is a large tropical American lizard with a crest of spines along its back.

clue.text: Resentment at busiest time, according to reports

indicators.note: reports are things heard, so the word is said aloud

parts.note: peak hours are the busiest time of day

explanation.surface: People resent the rush hour, by all accounts.
explanation.definitionFit: Pique is a fit of irritation from wounded pride, close to resentment.

clue.text: Not energetic? Stop suppressing energy

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down, so the energy letter is held within

parts.note: to quit is to stop
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Feeling lethargic? Stop holding in your energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something calm and low-key is not lively or energetic; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Nasty Thomas, dumping second girl in base operation

indicators.note: nasty signals the letters are messed up into a new order
dumping means getting rid of, so the letter for second goes

explanation.surface: Horrible Thomas ditches a second girlfriend at a military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dumping' drops S from THOMAS; 'Nasty' then rearranges THOMA with GIRL.
explanation.definitionFit: A logarithm is the power to which a fixed base number is raised, so finding one is an operation on a base.

clue.text: Esoteric expert, American, taken on by publication

indicators.note: taken on by means the second piece is added on after the first

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a publication
US means American, as in US troops

explanation.surface: An expert in the occult is hired by a magazine from America.
explanation.definitionFit: A magus is a sorcerer or wise man learned in occult lore, like the Magi of the Nativity.

clue.text: It's in zone abandoned by British in search of the best?

indicators.note: in means placed inside the next piece
abandoned by means the letter is left out of the word

parts.note: a belt is a zone, as in the commuter belt
it's is short for it is, written out in full

explanation.surface: A town region, deserted by Brits, still chases only the finest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' expands to IT IS. The definition has a question mark as the adjective loosely describes a seeker of quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone favouring only a select few, the top tier, is snobbishly devoted to the very best.

clue.text: One old lady with pizzazz is astonishing

parts.note: a means one, as in a dozen
old lady is slang for mother, ma
zing is energy and liveliness

explanation.surface: A spirited mum with plenty of flair stuns everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe something so remarkable that it causes great surprise or wonder.

clue.text: Rolling barrel? One must be crazy

indicators.note: rolling means turning over, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for beer or wine

explanation.surface: Anyone rolling a barrel around must be mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang calls an eccentric or insane person this, someone crazy.

clue.text: The scanner's broken? Charming woman!

indicators.note: broken means smashed into pieces, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that the scanner is broken, and then praises a lovely woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A witch who casts charms or spells, and by extension a captivating woman.
